uncited: CPU-Based Splat Sorting is a method for ordering volumetric primitives (specifically 3D Gaussian splats) by depth to enable correct front-to-back alpha blending.
It solves the problem of rendering transparency in splat-based volume visualization by ensuring that occluded splats do not incorrectly contribute to the final pixel color.
The method transforms splat positions into view space, extracts a depth metric, sorts the splats based on this metric, and outputs a permutation index buffer for the GPU renderer.
**Create Pairs:** Store the pair $(d_k, k)$ for all $k \in [0, N-1]$.
It differs from generic CPU sorting by leveraging vectorized instructions for parallel comparison and swapping.
It is chosen for web-based viewers requiring better performance than standard JS sorting while maintaining GPU offloading for rendering.
The GPU rendering phase remains $O(P)$ where $P$ is the number of pixels, but the CPU sort is a separate bottleneck.
*   Simplifies GPU shader logic (no need for complex sorting shaders or transform feedback).
*   Compatible with any hardware that supports basic OpenGL/WebGL rasterization.
*   Effective for static or slowly moving scenes.
*   Not suitable for real-time interactive applications requiring instant Z-order updates during fast navigation.
*   **When to Use:** Web-based viewers, legacy hardware, or scenes with static camera viewpoints.
*   **When Not to Use:** High-performance real-time VR/AR with rapid head movement, or scenes with >10M splats where CPU sort latency exceeds frame budget.

CPU-based splat sorting originated as a pragmatic solution for early web-based 3D Gaussian Splatting viewers, where GPU compute shaders were not universally available or efficient for sorting tasks [S1, unofficial].

It also notes that this approach was chosen because GPU sorting (like bitonic sort) requires many iterations and splitting GPU time between rendering and sorting is less efficient. This aligns with the claim that CPU-based sorting was a pragmatic solution for web-based viewers where GPU compute shaders were not universally available or efficient for sorting tasks.
